texts.orig: 2 Austin Downey's Perspective on Graduate School
texts.text: 2 Austin Downey's Perspective on Graduate School

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Graduate school represents a pivotal phase in one's professional journey. It is a time for intensive learning, significant growth, and meaningful contributions. As a professor with dual roles of Advisor and Project Manager, I see graduate school through two critical lenses: 1) the pursuit of studies and 2) the financial responsibilities attached to them. The second point leads to thinking of graduate school as employment; albeit a job focused on your success not company's finical gain.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.1 The Pursuit of Studies
texts.text: 2.1 The Pursuit of Studies

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Graduate school is an opportunity to develop deep technical skills in a chosen field while having the opportunity to explore complex problems and push the boundaries of knowledge. This demands dedication, hard work, and a genuine passion for research and learning. It is a period where you not only acquire advanced knowledge but also develop critical thinking, problem-solving skills, and the ability to work independently. The ultimate goal is to contribute new insights and innovations through scholarly work, culminating in published papers and presentations at conferences. This academic output is not just a measure of individual achievement but also a significant contribution to the broader scientific and academic community. As an advisor, my role is to help you through your academic journey. I provide intellectual support, help you navigate the complexities of your research, and offer feedback to ensure the quality and rigor of your work. I am here to help you develop your skills, identify opportunities, and overcome challenges in your studies. If your coursework is self-funded, the requirements for graduation are set by the Department of Mechanical Engineering Graduate Student Handbook.

texts.orig: 2.2 Financial Responsibilities
texts.text: 2.2 Financial Responsibilities

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Funding for graduate studies is very competitive and comes from sources through funded projects where I proposed a project and was awarded funds to carry out the research. When a sponsor provides financial support, it is not a mere act of charity. There are explicit expectations of return on investment. This return comes in the form of tangible outcomes, primarily publications. Broadly, these advancements hopefully lead to better lives for the citizenry, economic growth, and improved sustainability.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As a professor, I must emphasize the importance of understanding the differences between those who are self-funded and those who take financial support for their degrees. Accepting financial support carries a responsibility to deliver results. This means meeting project milestones, adhering to deadlines, and producing quality work that aligns with the sponsor's expectations. It is essential to view this relationship as a professional commitment, akin to a contractual agreement where both parties have obligations.

Accepting financial support carries a responsibility to deliver results. This means meeting project milestones, adhering to deadlines, and producing quality work that aligns with the sponsor's expectations. It is essential to view this relationship as a professional commitment, akin to a contractual agreement where both parties have obligations.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One crucial concept I stress is that graduation is not automatically granted when a student has been in the program for a certain amount of time or when funding runs out. Graduate school is not merely a matter of fulfilling course requirements as is done in undergrad. Rather it is about achieving specific academic and research goals. The culmination of graduate studies is marked by the successful completion of a body of work that meets the standards of the academic community and the expectations of the sponsors. Simply put, taking someone's money obligates the recipient to produce a product. In the academic context, this product is papers.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As a Project Manager, my role extends to overseeing the financial and operational aspects of research projects. I ensure that the resources provided by sponsors are utilized effectively and that project timelines and milestones are met. This involves coordinating tasks, monitoring progress, and maintaining clear communication between all stakeholders. My responsibility is to ensure that the project delivers the expected outcomes on time and that all commitments to sponsors are fulfilled. We must honor the trust and investment made by our sponsors. It is crucial to fulfill these commitments fully, reflecting both the values and the responsibilities of our academic community.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.3 Graduate School as Employment
texts.text: 2.3 Graduate School as Employment

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I encourage all new group members to think of themselves as employees rather than students. This perspective carries a different set of obligations. As a student, you are essentially a customer. You pay for classes and, in return, receive academic credit and, eventually, a degree. Your primary obligation is to yourself, ensuring you get a good return on your investment by doing the work and achieving good grades. As an employee, you are a vendor. Others pay you and expect to receive a product, whether it be a paper, or other published product. This mindset shift can change how you approach your responsibilities.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To that end, the group has the following policy. Students must spend at least eight hours per day on campus Monday through Friday. This helps instill an employee-like mindset while enabling collaboration. Being present on campus during regular business hours allows for face-toface interactions, fostering a professional environment and enhancing interactions between you and your colleagues. While remote work has become more common, this is an in-person lab.

texts.text: 3.2 Ph.D. Qualifying Examination

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The purpose of the Ph.D. Qualifying Examination is to ensure that students demonstrate the poten-tial to successfully complete a Ph.D. It is an assessment of capability and preparedness for doctor-al-level research (not a judgment of past accomplishments) and is therefore conducted early in the Ph.D. trajectory.
texts.text: The purpose of the Ph.D. Qualifying Examination is to ensure that students demonstrate the poten-tial to successfully complete a Ph.D. It is an assessment of capability and preparedness for doctor-al-level research (not a judgment of past accomplishments) and is therefore conducted early in the Ph.D. trajectory.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: All students, without extenuating circumstances, will complete the Ph.D. Qualifier in the Dynamics & Controls Track. This track requires a written assignment provided up to two weeks before the ex-am and an oral interaction based on that assignment. The qualifier must be completed within 12 months of the first graduate course taken (24 months for APOGEE students).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Qualifier Committee is composed of two or more faculty members. Dr. Downey will serve as one member, and the remaining members will generally be selected from the Department of Mechanical Engineering faculty who are positioned to support your research. These faculty members may or may not be members of your Ph.D. dissertation committee, as the qualifier and dissertation committees are separate entities. The Qualifier Committee will administer the written and oral parts of the exam.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The written portion of the qualifier consists of a single integrated process: when the qualifier is scheduled, the student must send their published first-author conference paper to all committee members. Faculty may then choose to provide written questions. These questions may be related to the paper or may be general qualifier questions. These questions are typically sent about one week before the exam. Students must return written responses (if any are assigned), cc'ing Dr. Downey, no later than 48 hours before the oral portion of the qualifier. Failure to return written responses 48 hours before the exam will result in automatic cancellation of the qualifier.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Student contributions: In the opening slides, students should provide a complete list of their publications, categorized into journals, peer-reviewed conferences, conferences, abstractonly publications, and posters. Students must also include a clear statement of their individual contributions to the field, recognizing that contributions at the qualifier stage may be limited in scope. This discussion should emphasize the student's intellectual role and technical ownership of multi-author papers to articulate to the committee your contributions (rather than team member contributions). Contribution statements may be compiled and merged from the itemized list and the end of the introduction in each section of the student's papers.

A short review of three to five journal papers would be ideal. Students should demonstrate an ability to summarize, compare, and critically assess existing approaches, rather than provide an exhaustive survey.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The Ph.D. Qualifier will result in one of three outcomes: pass, conditional pass, or fail. A pass indi-cates the student is prepared to proceed. A conditional pass requires the student to address specific concerns identified by the committee, which may include one-on-one follow-up meetings or written responses; the presentation will not be repeated. The committee will then determine an outcome of pass or fail, with all conditions resolved within two weeks. A fail indicates that the qualifier must be repeated in its entirety.

texts.orig: 3.3 Ph.D. Comprehensive Examination
texts.text: 3.3 Ph.D. Comprehensive Examination

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The comprehensive examination (also referred to as the proposal) evaluates a student's readiness to conduct independent dissertation research and judges their potential to complete a Ph.D., not mere-ly their past accomplishments. Before scheduling the exam, the student must have at least one pub-lished or accepted first-author, research-focused journal paper that helps frame and motivate the dissertation proposal. The comprehensive examination must be completed within 24 months of the first graduate course taken (36 months for APOGEE students).
texts.text: The comprehensive examination (also referred to as the proposal) evaluates a student's readiness to conduct independent dissertation research and judges their potential to complete a Ph.D., not mere-ly their past accomplishments. Before scheduling the exam, the student must have at least one pub-lished or accepted first-author, research-focused journal paper that helps frame and motivate the dissertation proposal. The comprehensive examination must be completed within 24 months of the first graduate course taken (36 months for APOGEE students).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The comprehensive exam requires both a written proposal and an oral defense. The written pro-posal should be approximately 15 pages in length and generally follow NSF proposal format re-quirements (see the NSF Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) guidance for structure and expectations). The written document must include: a clear background and motivation, three research objectives, and three tasks (each task mapped to one objective). It should also contain a timeline for the proposed work and a summary of prior work as needed to justify feasibility. The proposal will need to be shared with Dr. Downey through a Dropbox folder for review. A template for the Ph.D. proposal can be found here https://github.com/ARTS-Laboratory/ARTSLab-Ph.D.-Proposal-Template. The oral proposal defense is approximately 30 minutes in length and should follow a structure con-sistent with the Ph.D. Qualifier, but at a more advanced and forward-looking level. The purpose of the comprehensive examination is to evaluate readiness for independent dissertation research, not to present a completed dissertation.

The emphasis should be on technical clarity, logical alignment between objectives and tasks, and demonstration that the proposed work constitutes a coherent, Ph.D.-level research program. Unlike the qualifier, the comprehensive examination must present a well-defined and executable research plan. The committee will evaluate technical depth, feasibility, independence of thought, and the student's ability to defend methodological choices and anticipated contributions.

texts.orig: The final defense consists of a completed dissertation, a public presentation, and a closed-session question-and-answer portion with the committee. The public presentation is typically 40-45 minutes and should cover the overall research problem, gaps in the literature, the student's contributions, and the broader context of the work. It is crucial that students list all of their publications in the opening slides, clearly highlighting which publications are peer-reviewed, as consistent ac-ceptance by peers provides strong evidence of research quality. Students must also list their contri-butions to the field (again, taken from their papers) and are encouraged to refer back to these con-tributions throughout the presentation. The primary purpose of the committee during the defense is to ensure that the student has made meaningful contributions to their scientific field.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The ARTS-Lab is an interdisciplinary research lab at the University of South Carolina that is comprised of individuals working towards a progression in their chosen field. The ARTS-Lab is the people that make up the lab, not space or equipment. As such, well-trained researchers are our product. The following guidelines are intended to answer questions those (graduate and experienced undergraduate students) involved in the ARTS-Lab may have.

texts.orig: 7.1 Figures and Illustrations
texts.text: 7.1 Figures and Illustrations

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Software: Use Inkscape for creating and editing vector graphics and figures.
texts.text: Software: Use Inkscape for creating and editing vector graphics and figures.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Format: For optimal results in online publications, save figures as PNG files with a resolution of at least 300 DPI to ensure clarity and detail. If the figure contains photographic elements, using JPEG format at high-quality settings is appropriate. Avoid formats like PDF and SVG for final publication, as they can lead to larger file sizes and potential rendering issues.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · File size: To maintain control over the quality of your published work and prevent excessive compression by publishers, it's advisable to keep your entire paper's file size below 5 MB, with an absolute maximum of 10 MB. This approach minimizes the risk of the publisher applying additional compression that could degrade image quality.

This approach minimizes the risk of the publisher applying additional compression that could degrade image quality.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Capital letters in Figure Labels and Graphs: In our publications, we primarily use lowercase letters for labels in figures and graphs to enhance readability and maintain a clean visual presentation. This approach aligns with common practices where capitalization is reserved for proper nouns and the beginning of sentences. By using lowercase for most labels, we can effectively highlight specific elements when necessary by employing capitalization, such as for software titles or major items within a figure. This selective use of capital letters draws attention to significant components without overwhelming the reader by using bold text in figures.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · File Naming Conventions & the 'making_figures' Folder: For each paper, create a dedicated folder called making_figures. Within this folder, organize subfolders named exactly after each figure as it appears in your LaTeX document (e.g., Figure1, Figure2, etc.). Each of these subfolders should contain all data files, Inkscape files, and any other assets required to produce that specific figure. This approach not only enhances reproducibility, but also makes it much easier to share or update figures in the future.

Within this folder, organize subfolders named exactly after each figure as it appears in your LaTeX document (e.g., Figure1, Figure2, etc.). Each of these subfolders should contain all data files, Inkscape files, and any other assets required to produce that specific figure. This approach not only enhances reproducibility, but also makes it much easier to share or update figures in the future.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Copy Figures into a 'figures' Folder for LaTeX: Once you finalize a figure in its mak-ing_figures subfolder, place a copy of the final image file into a separate figures folder that your LaTeX document will reference. This way, you always know exactly which version of the figure is included in your paper, and you can easily provide the correct files when submitting to a journal. Keeping the 'making_figures' and 'figures' folders separate also serves as a helpful sanity check, ensuring you don't accidentally reference an outdated figure from somewhere else.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · No Spaces in Figure File Names: When naming your files or folders, do not use spaces. This is because many servers and systems (especially those running Linux) can encounter problems interpreting file paths with spaces, which may cause unexpected errors. Use underscores or CamelCase instead (e.g., Figure1_Draft or Figure1Draft). This practice is not only good computing hygiene but also ensures broader compatibility and fewer issues during file sharing or publication.
